Empirical Research Plan  
———————————————————  

1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: Sharp Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD).  
Justification: Treatment is mechanically assigned when an observable running (forcing) variable crosses a known cutoff. Around the cutoff, units are assumed to be as-good-as randomly assigned to treatment or control, satisfying the core RDD requirement that potential outcomes are smooth in the running variable in the absence of treatment. A sharp design is appropriate if compliance with the rule is perfect; if some units violate the rule, switch to a fuzzy RDD and scale the reduced-form estimate by the first-stage jump in treatment take-up.

2. Treatment and Control  
• Running variable (X): Continuous score that determines eligibility (e.g., test score, income, duration of unemployment).  
• Cutoff (c): Scalar constant c such that  
  Treatment = 1{ X ≥ c }  
• Treatment group: All observations with X ≥ c (just above the cutoff within a chosen bandwidth h).  
• Control group: Observations with X < c (just below the cutoff within h).  
• Timing: Cross-sectional RDD; if panel data exist, we use the first period after assignment as the outcome period to avoid contamination.  
Key constructed variables in the data set:  
 Treated ≡ (X ≥ c)  
 Running_c ≡ X – c (centered running variable)  
 Outcome ≡ Y (earnings, employment, etc.)

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff.  
Plausibility: The cutoff is an administrative rule unrelated to latent ability; small differences in X around c should not sharply change untreated outcomes.  
A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable.  
Plausibility: If X is a standardized score produced by a third party, manipulation costs are high. Testable via McCrary density test.  
A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers).  
Plausibility: Each individual’s outcome depends only on own treatment; reasonable if treatment capacity is not rationed across neighbors.  
A4. Treatment status is a deterministic function of X (sharp) or, in fuzzy designs, the first-stage jump is sizeable and monotone.  
A5. Covariates evolve smoothly at c.  
Plausibility: Check by running placebo RDs on pre-treatment covariates.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  
T1. Manipulation / sorting around the cutoff.  
 • Diagnostic: McCrary (2008) density test; visual histogram.  
 • Remedy: If manipulation is detected, tighten bandwidth, adopt local randomization RDD, or instrument actual treatment with the eligibility indicator (fuzzy RDD).  
T2. Functional-form / bandwidth sensitivity.  
 • Remedy: Report non-parametric local linear estimates with Imbens–Kalyanaraman (IK) optimal bandwidth; show robustness to ±50% bandwidth; present local quadratic as a sensitivity check.  
T3. Heterogeneous covariates or anticipation effects.  
 • Remedy: Balance tests on baseline covariates; placebo cutoffs away from c; if panel data exist, confirm that pre-treatment outcomes are flat at c.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(rdrobust)
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data
dat <- fread("threshold_data.csv")   # id, X (running var), Y (outcome), covariates...

# 2. Parameters
c <- 0                               # replace with actual cutoff

# 3. Construct key variables
dat[, running_c := X - c]
dat[, treat := (running_c >= 0)]

# 4. Main RD estimate (local linear, IK bandwidth)
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = dat$Y, x = dat$running_c, c = 0, p = 1, kernel = "triangular")
print(rd_main)

# 5. Plot RD graph (binned scatter)
bins <- 40
dat[, bin := cut(running_c, breaks = bins)]
plot_dat <- dat[, .(Ybar = mean(Y), Xbar = mean(running_c), N = .N), by = bin]
ggplot(plot_dat, aes(Xbar, Ybar)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
  geom_smooth(data = dat[running_c < 0], aes(running_c, Y),
              method = "lm", formula = y ~ running_c, se = FALSE, color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(data = dat[running_c >= 0], aes(running_c, Y),
              method = "lm", formula = y ~ running_c, se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Running variable (centered)", y = "Outcome")

# 6. Robustness check 1: bandwidth +/- 50%
bw_half <- rd_main$bws[1] / 2
bw_double <- rd_main$bws[1] * 2
rd_half  <- rdrobust(dat$Y, dat$running_c, h = bw_half)
rd_double <- rdrobust(dat$Y, dat$running_c, h = bw_double)

# 7. Robustness check 2: placebo cutoff 2 * bandwidth away
placebo_c <- 2 * rd_main$bws[1]
rd_placebo <- rdrobust(dat$Y, dat$running_c, c = placebo_c)

# 8. Covariate balance example
rd_cov <- rdrobust(y = dat$covariate1, x = dat$running_c)
```

6. Expected Results  
Economic priors depend on the specific intervention. For a job-training program awarded above the cutoff, theory predicts higher employment probability and higher earnings. Magnitude: a local average treatment effect (LATE) of +5–10 percentage-point increase in employment rate, or +5–15% increase in annual earnings among compliers.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  
C1: Density of running variable smooth at cutoff (McCrary) … 1  
C2: Baseline covariates continuous at cutoff … 1  
C3: Chosen bandwidth passes robustness checks … 1  
C4: Treatment assignment obeys rule / no cross-overs (sharp) … 0.8  
C5: Outcome model specification (polynomial order, kernel) does not drive results … 0.8  
Overall score ≈ 4.6 / 5 → high internal validity, subject to usual local‐external‐validity trade-off.

This plan provides a transparent roadmap to estimate treatment effects induced by a threshold rule and demonstrates how to probe and document the key assumptions underlying an RDD.
